questions.question: Which of these requirements is a cross-cutting concern?
options: Calculating the discount for an order based on the customer's loyalty tier
Deciding which fields are mandatory when a new student is created
Recording the start, end and failure of method calls in the student, order and payment services
Computing the refund amount when a payment is cancelled
questions.explanation: A concern is cross-cutting when the same kind of behaviour is needed across many unrelated modules. Method-execution logging applies to student, order and payment services alike. The other options are business rules that belong to a single domain (orders, students, payments).

questions.question: In the lecture's "what / where / when" model of AOP, the rule "apply only to methods annotated with `@TrackExecutionTime`" is an example of which concept?
options: Pointcut: it selects WHERE the extra behaviour applies
Advice: it describes WHAT extra action runs
Advice type: it decides WHEN the action runs relative to the method
Target: it is the real object holding the business logic
questions.explanation: A pointcut is the rule that selects which method executions are affected (the 'where'). The advice is the action itself, such as measuring time (the 'what'). The advice type (before, after, around…) is the 'when'. The target is the advised bean, not a selection rule.

questions.question: Two complaints come up in a code review. (A) "Changing the log format means editing about 100 methods across 20 services." (B) "`processPayment()` mixes logging, permission checks, timing and auditing around one line of real payment logic." Which labels are correct?
options: (A) is tangling and (B) is scattering
Both are scattering, because the same logging code appears in many places
Both are tangling, because business and infrastructure code are mixed
(A) is scattering and (B) is tangling
questions.explanation: Scattering means one concern's code is spread across many locations, so a policy change touches many classes (A). Tangling means one method contains code from several unrelated concerns, which hides its business intent (B). They are two different problems that cross-cutting code usually causes together.

questions.question: A teammate says: "We moved all logging into `LoggingServiceUtil.logStart()` and `logEnd()`, so the cross-cutting problem is solved." What problem still remains?
options: Static utility methods cannot be called from Spring beans, so logging will not run at all
Every business method must still call the utility, so WHERE and WHEN logging applies stays scattered and can be forgotten or applied inconsistently
The logging implementation is now duplicated in every class that calls the utility
The utility makes each service method run twice, once for logging and once for the business logic
questions.explanation: A utility centralises WHAT the concern does, but the invocation stays in every method. Developers must remember `logStart`/`logEnd` (and the try/catch for failures), which keeps the code scattered and error-prone. The implementation itself is not duplicated, and static methods are perfectly callable from beans.

questions.question: In the lecture project, `StudentController` gets a `StudentService` injected and calls `createStudent(student)`. The beans are wired as shown. What is printed (ignoring the exact millisecond value)?
options: Executing -> ..., Student saved, Finishing -> ..., then the elapsed time
The elapsed time, then Executing -> ..., Student saved, Finishing -> ...
Student saved only, because the controller is injected with `StudentServiceImpl`
Executing -> ..., Finishing -> ..., Student saved, then the elapsed time
questions.explanation: `@Primary` makes Spring inject `ExecutionTimeService` (the outermost wrapper) into the controller. It starts the timer and delegates to `LoggingDecorator`, which logs start, calls the real `StudentServiceImpl` ("Student saved"), and logs finish. Control then returns and the elapsed time is printed last. This is the manual wrapper chain that Spring AOP later automates.

questions.question: Why does putting `logStart()`/`logEnd()` in an abstract `BaseService` that all services extend NOT solve the cross-cutting problem?
options: Protected methods in an abstract class cannot be called by subclasses in another package
Spring cannot create beans for classes that extend an abstract class
Inheritance only shares the code; each method must still call it manually, and Java's single inheritance forces unrelated services into one artificial hierarchy
Subclasses would execute the base-class logging automatically before every method, so it would run twice
questions.explanation: A base class gives subclasses access to shared methods but never runs them automatically around selected methods, so the calls stay scattered. It also uses up Java's single superclass slot and tends to grow into a bloated class mixing logging, security and so on. Protected members are accessible to subclasses in any package, and Spring handles such beans fine.

questions.question: In the lecture project, someone deletes the `@Primary` annotation from `ExecutionTimeService`. Nothing else changes. What happens when the application starts?
options: It starts and injects `StudentServiceImpl`, because `@Service` beans are preferred over `@Component` beans
Startup fails: three beans implement `StudentService` and none is primary or matches the parameter name, so the controller's dependency is ambiguous (`NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`)
It starts and injects whichever implementation was scanned first
Startup fails because `LoggingDecorator` cannot be injected with the concrete `StudentServiceImpl` type
questions.explanation: The controller asks for `StudentService`, and three candidates exist: `executionTimeService`, `loggingDecorator` and `studentServiceImpl`. Without `@Primary` (or `@Qualifier`, or a matching parameter name) Spring cannot choose and fails with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Spring never prefers `@Service` over `@Component` or picks the first scanned bean, and injecting by a concrete class type is fine because only one bean has that type.

questions.question: What does this manual-wrapper program print?
options:
Method started
Caught: DB down

Method started
Method finished
Saved

Caught: DB down
Method finished

Method started
Method finished
Caught: DB down
questions.explanation: The wrapper prints "Method started", then delegates to the target, which throws. The `finally` block still runs ("Method finished") before the exception propagates to `main`, where it is caught. Neither the println of the result nor "Saved" runs. This before/delegate/after shape is exactly what an AOP proxy automates.

questions.question: A logging aspect correctly logs `StudentService.createStudent()` when called from the controller. In a unit-style helper, a developer writes `StudentService s = new StudentService(repo); s.createStudent(st);` and no log appears. Why?
options: Spring AOP works by handing callers a Spring-created proxy around a Spring-managed bean; an object built with `new` is the plain target, so nothing intercepts the call
Aspects only run for methods called from a `@RestController`
The aspect is applied lazily, and the first call to any bean is never advised
Calling the constructor directly removes the pointcut annotation from the class at runtime
questions.explanation: Advice runs because the caller holds a proxy that Spring created and injected; the proxy runs the advice and delegates to the real target. `new StudentService(...)` bypasses the IoC container, so the caller has the raw target and no proxy is involved. Being called from a controller has nothing to do with it; what matters is whether the call goes through the proxy.

questions.question: Your app has three unrelated service interfaces (`StudentOperations`, `OrderOperations`, `PaymentOperations`), and each needs security, logging, timing and auditing. Using only hand-written, interface-specific decorators like the lecture's `LoggingStudentService`, how many wrapper classes do you need, and what does AOP change?
options: 4 wrappers (one per concern); AOP only removes the need to order them
3 wrappers (one per interface); AOP removes the need for interfaces
12 wrappers (4 concerns x 3 interfaces), each assembled in the right order by hand; with AOP each concern is one aspect whose pointcut selects the methods
7 wrappers (4 + 3); AOP merges them into a single proxy class written by the developer
questions.explanation: A decorator implements one specific interface, so `LoggingStudentService` cannot wrap `OrderOperations`. Each concern needs a wrapper per interface (4 x 3 = 12), plus manual nesting and injection of the outermost layer. AOP keeps each concern in one aspect, uses pointcuts to choose the methods, and lets Spring generate and integrate the proxies.
